prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opening moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: Twisted bilayer graphene is the cleanest recent example of what I look for: a continuum-model prediction (2011) of flat bands at a magic angle, followed seven years later by correlated insulators and superconductivity at exactly that angle. The theory-experiment loop is direct, and the result is a genuine surprise in a material, much as stable graphene was in 2004. It has been reproduced by many groups, including in other moire platforms (other twisted and heterostructure systems with correlated and topological states), so the core discovery does not rest on one laboratory. Electronic-structure theory has also been able to engage quantitatively with it, which is what I ask of a mature condensed-matter result. Six of the seven members who ranked it placed it in their top three, and the support is spread across condensed-matter, atomic and astroparticle members rather than coming from one subfield.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, device-to-device variation from twist-angle disorder is real, and several correlated phases are still being assigned. A committee could reasonably say the field is eight years old and that a prize now rewards the platform before its physics is settled. A second concern is attribution: the first experimental authors (Cao, Fatemi and colleagues) cannot be credited, other groups (Dean, Young, Watanabe and Taniguchi crystals) contributed to the broader area, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) preceded the 2011 calculation. By comparison, the optical lattice clock is further along in maturity and has cleaner attribution.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the lattice clock first and puts twisted graphene second with MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero only, noting that Bistritzer's equal role in the 2011 calculation is a real credit question and that the pairing mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree the pairing mechanism is open, but I do not think it should block recognition: the discovery is the existence of flat-band-driven correlated and superconducting phases, which is established, and the Nobel Committee has honoured discoveries before their mechanism was understood. On credit I disagree with dropping Bistritzer. The 2011 paper is a joint Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation and the magic-angle prediction is the theoretical half of the story. Leaving him out would split a single paper, and a three-person prize is within the rules. I would sooner accept the allocation difficulty on the experimental side, where students necessarily go unnamed, than weaken the theory credit.

responses.point: Lindroth puts optical lattice clocks first because light shifts are cancelled by design, atomic theory and experiment agree to extraordinary precision, and many laboratories have reproduced the 1e-18 level; she places twisted graphene fifth and defers to condensed-matter colleagues.
responses.response: I take the robustness argument seriously, and I ranked B007 fifth only because it is an invention and precision-measurement achievement rather than a new state of matter, not because I doubt it. My reservation is the overlap you flag yourself with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize: a committee that has twice rewarded the precision-spectroscopy chain may feel this is a third step. Twisted graphene opens a field with no earlier prize, and the independent replication across many groups answers the question of whether it is a stable result. I would be comfortable with B007 as a serious alternative, and I do not think the two cases are in conflict if the committee later wants a two-part prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened a new observational window, and notes that source associations such as TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are evidence-level and that credit within a very large collaboration is hard to apportion.
responses.response: I defer to you on astroparticle physics, and the new-window argument is a strong one. My concern is the one you state: the source identifications are evidence-level, the credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and several hundred collaborators is difficult, and no third name is as clear-cut as Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero are for the moire case. I would want the committee to say what exactly the prize citation would reward, the diffuse flux or the source identifications, before putting B039 ahead of a candidate with a cleaner three-name structure. Your own ranking of twisted graphene third suggests you do not find the condensed-matter case weak.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted graphene first on the grounds that a simple analytical continuum model made a general prediction that was tested directly in experiment, though priority for earlier twisted-bilayer theory is unverified.
responses.response: We agree on the central argument. On the priority point, I think the Bistritzer-MacDonald contribution is the specific, quantitative prediction of the magic angle and the flat-band condition, which earlier work on moire superlattices did not provide, so I find the credit defensible, though the citation should be worded around the magic-angle flat bands so as not to claim all twisted-bilayer theory. I would also stress that the moire case has a direct experimental verification of the predicted flat-band regime, which is what makes it more robust than purely model-driven universality arguments.

responses.point: Johansson ranks twisted graphene third and the topological insulator candidate eighth, noting that the 2016 prize on topological phases may already cover part of that ground.
responses.response: I disagree with the idea that the 2016 prize covers B023. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and topological phases in the quantum-Hall and one-dimensional context. Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the Z2 classification are a different, experimentally confirmed development, now textbook, with ARPES and transport confirmation. I place B023 as my own second choice, and I would flag the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap in its credit, but I do not think overlap with 2016 is disqualifying.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee will give to the unresolved pairing mechanism and device-to-device reproducibility when judging maturity.

Whether the supplied three-name credit (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) is the fairest, given Cao and other first experimental authors and earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos and colleagues.
Whether the topological-insulator candidate B023 should be preferred if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit gap can be handled in a citation.
Whether the lattice clock, which has the broadest opening support, is regarded as a discovery or an instrument advance after the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the shortlisted candidates involves my Uppsala group, Los Alamos collaborators, my doctoral supervisor or the co-authors of my monographs. I work in electronic-structure theory and magnetism, close to but not overlapping with the moire-materials community, and I note that closeness to avoid bias.
